paras: The killing of William Beardsley took place on August 7, 1910, when Deputy Sheriff William Nugent shot and killed Beardsley, a Black man, in a freight car in the N. O., M. and C. Railroad yards at Mobile, Alabama. Nugent and a second deputy had come to arrest him on an assault charge, and the only reports found, all in the Montgomery Advertiser, described the shooting as self-defense. Bessie Cannon, a Black woman who was in the car, was afterward held for the grand jury on a charge of assault to murder.

According to the Advertiser's Mobile correspondent, Beardsley was wanted on a charge of assault and battery. A later dispatch said he was wanted for assaulting Cannon's mother in the latter part of April. The first report gave his name as "Will Beaslel" and "Beasley"; the later ones called him Beardsley, and the August 11 item gave his full name as William Beardsley.

On Sunday, August 7, Nugent and a second deputy went to arrest Beardsley in a box car in the railroad yards. In the account printed on August 9, Cannon had warned the deputies of "the desperate nature of the man they wanted," and as the officers started to enter the car Beardsley appeared at the door and pointed his pistol at Nugent until Deputy Gillis knocked his hand up. A struggle for the pistol followed in a corner of the car, during which Cannon is said to have told Beardsley to shoot Nugent.

When Beardsley had placed his weapon nearly against a deputy's stomach, Nugent fired, fatally wounding him; the printed text is partly illegible at this point. The first report, of August 8, put it more simply: Beasley shot at the officer, who returned the fire with fatal effect.

Cannon was held for assault to murder on August 8, and on August 10 she was held for the action of the grand jury at Mobile. No report of a coroner's inquest, of any official finding on the killing, or of Cannon's later prosecution appears in the coverage.

The three reports found were brief special dispatches from Mobile printed in the Montgomery Advertiser on August 8, 9 and 11, 1910. Each gave the deputies' version as fact: the first ran under the headline "DEPUTY KILLS NEGRO WHO RESISTS ARREST" and said Nugent killed him "in self-defense," and the second called Beardsley "the negro desperado" whom Nugent "was forced to kill." The August 9 story centered on Cannon rather than the dead man, under the headline "NEGRESS HELD FOR ASSAULT" and the subhead "Was With Desperado in Box Car Battle."

By August 11 the case had become a paragraph in a column of Mobile court news, following an item on prohibition cases. No account from Beardsley's side or from Cannon, and no coverage in the Black press, was found.

The reports disagree on the second deputy: the August 9 account named him as Gillis and had him knock up Beardsley's hand and close with him, while the August 11 account named Deputy Sheriff Stogsdill and said he struggled hand to hand with Beardsley for the gun while Cannon interfered with Nugent. The August 9 account also placed Nugent himself in the hand-to-hand struggle and said Beardsley had tried to kill Gillis. The first report said Beardsley shot at Nugent, while the fuller account of the next day described him pointing his pistol but did not say he fired.
